pinterest.title: Greek Wedding Traditions in Order: From the Engagement to the Kalamatianos
pinterest.description: Greek wedding traditions come in two layers. The Orthodox service is set by the Church: the betrothal and rings, the candles, the crowning with stefana, the common cup and the Dance of Isaiah. Around it sit family customs that vary by region, from the krevati to names on the bride's shoe and koufeta for guests. Our guide walks 12 customs in the order a couple meets them, and says plainly which are simply often told.

pinterest.title: What Do the Stefana Mean? The Crowning in a Greek Orthodox Wedding
pinterest.description: The crowning is usually described as the centre of the Greek Orthodox wedding service. The stefana are two crowns, usually joined by a ribbon, and the koumbaros usually exchanges them over the couple's heads three times. The Church explains them as crowns of God's glory. There are no spoken vows, so tell your photographer this is the moment to watch. Read the full guide to Greek wedding traditions.

pinterest.title: Koufeta: Why Greek Weddings Give Sugared Almonds in Odd Numbers
pinterest.description: Koufeta are white sugared almonds, found on the ceremony tray, at each place setting and in the bomboniere guests take home. They are usually given in odd numbers, and the reason often told is that an odd number cannot be divided, like the couple. Another story says an unmarried guest who sleeps with koufeta under the pillow will dream of a future spouse. More Greek wedding traditions in our guide.

slides: Greek wedding traditions come in two layers. Do you know which is which?
Layer one: the Orthodox service, set by the Church. Layer two: the family customs around it, which vary by family and region.
No vows. The Orthodox Church describes marriage as a sacrament with no vows or oaths. The crowning, not a kiss, is the moment most guests watch for.
The stefana: two crowns, usually joined by a ribbon, usually exchanged over the couple's heads three times by the koumbaros.
Then the common cup, usually sipped three times, and the Dance of Isaiah: the priest leads the crowned couple three times around the ceremony table.
Around the service, the folklore is often told: friends make the marriage bed (krevati), single friends sign the bride's shoe, and koufeta come in odd numbers.
At the reception: the kalamatianos circle dance, a chorus of "na zisete", a wish for a long life together, and ftou ftou, meant kindly.

instagram_carousel.caption:
Most lists of Greek wedding traditions mix two different things. One is the Orthodox service, a sacrament with its own order and its own meaning. The other is the family folklore around it, which changes from family to family and island to island.

Inside the church, as the service is usually described: the betrothal and rings, the candles, the crowning with stefana, the Gospel and the common cup, and the Dance of Isaiah. There are no spoken vows at any point. If you want personal words, the reception speeches are the natural place for them.

Around it, the customs are often told rather than written down: the krevati, names on the bride's shoe, koufeta in odd numbers, and the bride said to step on the groom's foot so she has the last word.

Our guide takes 12 customs in the order a couple meets them, plus what Australians need to know about marrying legally in Greece as at November 2026, and about holding the same service in a parish at home. Link in bio.
